dedupe_keys.name: leadership void for climate adaptation planning at the port of providence rhode island becker and kretsch 2019

description: A study by the University of Rhode Island of who should lead climate adaptation at the Port of Providence, published in Frontiers in Earth Science in 2019. Coverage: the multi-owner port of Providence, Rhode Island, which has no central port authority. Methods: after an August 2015 hurricane resilience workshop that used visualisations of storm impacts, 31 private and public stakeholders were invited to an online survey and interviews between February and May 2016 on where leadership for adaptation should sit. Outcome: stakeholders knew the risks from storms and sea level rise but could not agree who is responsible, who pays or on what timescale, a leadership void that the authors identify as a main barrier to resilience planning; facilitated dialogue was valued as a first step. Format and access: open article with tables and figures. Licence and cost: CC BY 4.0, free. Caveats: a single port and a small group of respondents, with qualitative results. It is useful context for climate adaptation and resilience models of ports where many owners share assets and decisions. It relates to the Port of Los Angeles sea level rise study and the Port of London Authority adaptation report in the catalogue.

name: Leadership void for climate adaptation planning at the Port of Providence, Rhode Island (Becker and Kretsch, 2019)
outcomes: Stakeholders saw no clear owner of port resilience: an institutional leadership void, with no port authority to plan, left unclear who should lead and pay for adaptation; respondents valued facilitated dialogue as a first step.
